Information Criteria for Structural Equation Models

Source: R/sem_information_criteria.R
sem_information_criteria.Rd

Computes the information criteria used to choose among structural equation models fitted to the same data: AIC (Akaike, 1974), BIC (Schwarz, 1978), the sample size adjusted BIC (SABIC; Sclove, 1987), Haughton's (1988) BIC (HBIC), and the information matrix based BIC (IBIC) and scaled unit information prior BIC (SPBIC) that Bollen, Ray, Zavisca, and Harden (2012) proposed and Bollen, Harden, Ray, and Zavisca (2014) evaluated for structural equation models. Each criterion is minus twice the maximized log likelihood plus a penalty for the free parameters, smaller values are preferred, and only the difference between two models fitted to the same data under the same likelihood carries meaning. The function takes either a fitted lavaan model, whose log likelihood, parameter count, sample size, and (for IBIC and SPBIC) information matrices it reads, or those quantities as summary input, so that a published comparison can be reproduced. compare_sem compares a set of fitted models by one criterion. A fitted model requires lavaan (in Suggests).

Usage

sem_information_criteria(
  fit = NULL,
  log_likelihood = NULL,
  npar = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  measures = c("AIC", "BIC", "SABIC", "HBIC"),
  parameter_estimate = NULL,
  prior_mean = NULL,
  zero_parameters = NULL,
  information_observed = NULL,
  information_expected = NULL,
  information_scale = c("total", "per_observation"),
  spbic_dimension = NULL
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted lavaan model: a maximum likelihood fit of continuous variables under the normal likelihood (estimator ML or its robust variants MLM, MLMV, and MLR) that converged to an admissible solution, as sem_fit_measures judges it. See Details for what is refused. Supply either fit or the summary input below, not both.

log_likelihood

For summary input, the maximized log likelihood \(\ell\), including its constants (lavaan's logl).

npar

For summary input, the number d of independent free parameters of the likelihood whose maximum is log_likelihood, a positive whole number, counted the same way for every model to be compared. A fitted model supplies lavaan's count, attr(logLik(fit), "df"), which leaves out the saturated means of a model without a mean structure and, under fixed.x = TRUE, the moments of the exogenous observed variables; a difference between two models with the same settings is unaffected.

N

For summary input, the sample size N in the penalties of the BIC family, greater than 1. A fitted model supplies its total over groups.

measures

The criteria to compute: any of "AIC", "BIC", "SABIC", "HBIC", "IBIC", and "SPBIC", in either case. The default computes the four that need only \(\ell\), d, and N. Every row of the table is reported whatever is requested, with NA for a criterion not computed.

parameter_estimate

For SPBIC from summary input, the vector \(\hat{\theta}\) of the d free parameter estimates, in the order of the rows of information_observed.

prior_mean

For SPBIC, the vector \(\theta^*\) of prior means, in the order of parameter_estimate. Supply this or zero_parameters. With a fitted model and neither, the rule of Bollen et al. (2014, p. 6) applies: free loadings and regression coefficients are centered at zero and every other free parameter at its estimate (see Details).

zero_parameters

For SPBIC, the positions or unique names of the entries of parameter_estimate to center at zero, every other entry being centered at its estimate. A saturated model needs an explicit choice; Bollen et al. (2014, p. 6) center its covariances at zero and its variances (and means) at their estimates.

information_observed

For SPBIC from summary input, the observed information matrix \(I_O(\hat{\theta})\): the negative Hessian of the log likelihood at the estimates, in the free parameters, in the order of parameter_estimate.

information_expected

For IBIC from summary input, the expected (Fisher) information matrix \(I_E(\hat{\theta})\) at the estimates, in the free parameters. The inverse of a robust (sandwich) covariance matrix of the estimates is not an information matrix and is no substitute.

information_scale

For summary input, whether the supplied information matrices are for the whole sample ("total", the default; the inverse of the covariance matrix of the estimates under ML) or per observation ("per_observation", what lavaan::lavInspect() reports), in which case they are multiplied by N. A fitted model supplies per observation matrices, which are multiplied by N, and the argument is refused with one.

spbic_dimension

Optional: the dimension used in the penalty of SPBIC, a positive whole number no greater than npar. By default it is npar, as in the general expression. Bollen et al.'s (2014) Table 6 used smaller counts for SPBIC, printed in parentheses (15 for the saturated model rather than 20), and states no rule for them; supply such a count only to reproduce that table, never to tune a ranking. It changes neither parameter_estimate nor the information matrices.

Value

A dmar_tbl (class dmar_sem_information) with columns term and value and, always in this order, the rows AIC, BIC, SABIC, HBIC, IBIC, and SPBIC (NA for a criterion not requested), log_likelihood, npar, and N. The sem_information attribute records the source; for a fitted model the likelihood, the missing data method, the exogenous observed variables it conditions on, the mean structure, the number of groups, and, when IBIC or SPBIC is computed, the identification of each latent variable; the scale and provenance of the information matrices; the log determinant of the whole sample expected information for IBIC; for SPBIC the estimates, the prior means and the rule that set them, Q, the penalty dimension and its rule, the penalty, and whether the boundary branch applied; for a two-stage fit whose first stage read cases observed on an auxiliary variable alone, two_stage_rows, the cases read and lavaan's count of them in each group, how many such cases there are, whether the fit was computed again with all of them (corrected), and whether its estimates depend on the counts, so that they were computed again too (reestimated); and the lines of the printed footer.

Details

The Criteria

Write \(\ell\) for the maximized log likelihood, d for the number of free parameters, and N for the sample size. Each criterion is \(-2\ell\) plus a penalty: \(AIC = -2\ell + 2d\) (Akaike, 1974), \(BIC = -2\ell + d\log N\) (Schwarz, 1978), \(SABIC = -2\ell + d\log\{(N + 2)/24\}\) (Sclove, 1987; lavaan's bic2), and \(HBIC = -2\ell + d\log\{N/(2\pi)\}\) (Haughton, 1988).

Bollen et al. (2012) derive the BIC family from the Laplace approximation to the log of a model's marginal likelihood, $$\log P(Y|M) = \ell + \log P(\hat{\theta}|M) + \frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{d}{2}\log N - \frac{1}{2}\log|\bar{I}_E(\hat{\theta})| + O(N^{-1/2})$$ (Bollen et al., 2014, Eq. 9), where \(P(\hat{\theta}|M)\) is the prior density at the estimates and \(\bar{I}_E = I_E/N\) the expected information per observation. Multiplied by \(-2\), BIC keeps the first and fourth terms, HBIC the third as well, and IBIC every term but the prior: \(IBIC = -2\ell + d\log\{N/(2\pi)\} + \log|\bar{I}_E(\hat{\theta})|\) (Bollen et al., 2012, Eq. 20; 2014, Eq. 16), which equals \(-2\ell - d\log(2\pi) + \log|I_E(\hat{\theta})|\) for the whole sample information. Recomputing the worked example of Bollen et al. (2012, Table 1) from its printed inputs shows that the log determinant it adds to \(d\log\{N/(2\pi)\}\) is that of the whole sample information (its elements are about \(N\) times the per observation ones the log likelihood implies), which counts \(\log N\) twice relative to their Eq. 20; this function follows Eq. 20, which reproduces the IBIC row of Bollen et al. (2014, Table 6).

SPBIC replaces BIC's unit information prior with a normal prior centered at \(\theta^*\) (prior_mean) whose variance, a multiple of the inverse unit information, is chosen to maximize the marginal likelihood, an empirical Bayes prior. With \(Q = (\hat{\theta} - \theta^*)' I_O(\hat{\theta}) (\hat{\theta} - \theta^*)\) for the estimates \(\hat{\theta}\) (parameter_estimate) and the whole sample observed information \(I_O\), \(SPBIC = -2\ell + d\{1 + \log(Q/d)\}\) when \(Q > d\) (Bollen et al., 2012, Eq. 14; 2014, Eq. 18). When \(Q \le d\) the maximizing prior variance is zero, the prior is a point mass at \(\theta^*\), and \(SPBIC = -2\ell + Q\) (Bollen et al., 2012, Eq. 15); the two branches meet at \(Q = d\). Bollen et al. (2014, note 7) never met that branch and caution that its behavior is little known, and the function warns when it applies.

SABIC replaces N in BIC's penalty with \((N + 2)/24\), the penalty of Rissanen's (1978) shortest data description criterion as Sclove (1987, criteria 4 and 5) gives it, which comes from the length of a coded description of the data rather than from the Laplace approximation; Lin, Huang, and Weng (2017) write it ABIC, and Mplus and lavaan's bic2 call it the sample size adjusted BIC. Its penalty per parameter is smaller than BIC's, and it is not positive when \(N \le 22\), where the function warns. Lin et al. (2017) found that it improved on BIC in selecting path models mainly with small samples or small misspecifications, and that HBIC and SPBIC did best overall. AIC estimates the relative expected Kullback-Leibler discrepancy of a model rather than its marginal likelihood (Burnham & Anderson, 2004). AICc is not offered: its correction is derived for the univariate linear model and is not justified for structural equation models in general.

Units and Identification

AIC, BIC, SABIC, and HBIC depend on a model only through \(\ell\) and d, which do not change when an observed variable is rescaled or a latent variable is identified another way. IBIC and SPBIC also depend on the information matrix in the free parameters as they are parameterized.

IBIC keeps \(\log|\bar{I}_E|\) but drops the prior density of the Laplace approximation, and that is the term whose Jacobian would cancel a change of parameterization. When the units of a free parameter are multiplied by \(c^k\), \(\log|\bar{I}_E|\) changes by \(-2k\log c\). Rescaling an observed variable by c therefore changes the IBIC of one model relative to another by \(-2k\log c\) for each free parameter the first has and the second lacks whose units carry that variable's (\(k = 1\) for a loading or for a covariance with an unscaled variable, \(k = 2\) for its variance), and the ranking of two models fitted to the same data can reverse when one variable's units change. Identifying the latent variables by fixing their variances (std.lv = TRUE) rather than by a marker indicator changes IBIC differences too, since the map between the two parameterizations is nonlinear and its Jacobian differs between models. An IBIC comparison is defined only for a stated choice of units and identification. Standardizing every observed variable before fitting every model, or keeping their original metrics, fixes the units, but it is a convention rather than an invariant answer: report it, and read IBIC beside BIC, HBIC, and SPBIC.

SPBIC's Q is invariant to a linear reparameterization when the prior mean is transformed with the estimates, so rescaling an observed variable does not change it under the default prior. That prior, however, centers the free loadings and regression coefficients at zero and the other free parameters at their estimates, and which parameters are free loadings depends on the identification: under std.lv = TRUE every loading is centered at zero, while under a marker indicator, the convention of the example of Bollen et al. (2014), the scale sits in the factor variance, which stays at its estimate. A mean structure adds the saturated means to d, and their information to \(\bar{I}_E\). Models compared by IBIC or SPBIC must therefore share their identification and mean structure; compare_sem requires every latent variable of every model to be identified the same way (each by a marker indicator, or each by a fixed variance) and the same mean structure, and refuses a set that does not, and for a fitted model the sem_information attribute records both.

What a Fitted Model Supplies

\(\ell\) is lavaan's logLik(fit), d its df attribute, and N the total sample size. In a multiple group model \(\ell\) is the sum over the groups and N the total, as in lavaan. Under fixed.x = TRUE (the default of lavaan::sem()) or conditional.x = TRUE, \(\ell\) is the log likelihood conditional on the exogenous observed variables, and criteria compare only models with the same exogenous variables. Under FIML (missing = "ml") \(\ell\) is the observed data log likelihood. Under missing = "two.stage" or "robust.two.stage" it is the complete data normal log likelihood at the stage one EM estimates of the means and covariances, so that AIC and BIC are the two-stage criteria of Lai (2021, Eqs. 32 and 35), up to a constant shared by all models fitted to the same data; Lai shows that, unlike the FIML criteria, they select in large samples the model complete data would select when the values are missing at random, and that in samples of the usual size they miss it more often than complete data would. They are comparable only with other two-stage fits of the same variables with the same auxiliary variables in the first stage, and they are the AIC and BIC rows fa_confirmatory reports after two-stage estimation. For IBIC and SPBIC, the expected and observed information matrices are lavaan's per observation lavInspect(fit, "information.expected") and lavInspect(fit, "information.observed"), multiplied by N; they are the matrices the criteria are defined on under lavaan's defaults h1.information = "structured" (the expected information at the fitted moments) and observed.information = "hessian" (the negative Hessian), and other settings are refused.

A two-stage fit can have cases observed on an auxiliary variable (lavaan's aux) but on none of the model's variables. lavaan's first stage reads them, so they move the EM estimates, but its sample size (lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "nobs")) counts them as empty and leaves them out, and it forms the log likelihood as that sample size times the complete data log likelihood per case at the EM estimates. Its log likelihood, and the N of the penalties of BIC, SABIC, and HBIC, then rest on fewer cases than the moments. Both are computed here from the fit computed again with every case the first stage read: in one group, and in several groups that no constraint holds together, the estimates do not depend on the count, and the log likelihood of each group is its value per case times the cases its first stage read, with N their total. A line under the table says so, and the sem_information attribute records the counts. On six Holzinger and Swineford tests with the whole block missing for 77 of 301 pupils, at random given general information (the auxiliary), lavaan's N for the two-factor model is 224 and its log likelihood -4040.25, which is 224/301 of the -5429.09 reported here with N = 301 (BIC 10966.61 here, 8183.32 from lavaan's values). In several groups held together by a constraint, such as equal loadings or intercepts, the second stage weights each group by its count, so when the groups' counts grow in different ratios the estimates move as well, and the log likelihood is the one at the estimates with every case read (those of semTools' twostage()), which the line says. On the same tests by school with equal loadings and intercepts (130 and 94 cases with an observed test, 156 and 145 read), it is -5393.34 with BIC 10957.89, against -5393.52 and 10958.25 at lavaan's estimates and -4020.79 and 8203.92 from lavaan's values. fa_confirmatory(missing = "two_stage") and measurement_invariance return fits that count the cases already, and give the same criteria. FIML (missing = "ml") keeps the cases in its likelihood and in N as well.

What Is Refused

A fitted model is refused when it did not converge or has an improper solution, when it has ordered categorical indicators or was fitted by an estimator other than ML (its fit function is then not a log likelihood), when it uses the Wishart likelihood, and when it was fitted with sampling weights: lavaan then maximizes a weighted pseudo log likelihood (Asparouhov, 2005), for which neither the penalties nor the information matrices have their likelihood justification. For a two-level model the sample size in the BIC family's penalty is ambiguous (Bollen et al., 2012, p. 295), so only AIC is computed from the fit, and the others need summary input with the N the user chooses. Automatic IBIC and SPBIC further need a single group, single level ML fit (not MLM or MLR) of complete data whose free parameters are unconstrained, with no exploratory (rotated) blocks (their information matrices are singular) and with the exogenous observed variables modeled (fixed.x = FALSE). Each refusal says why and what to do; for another parameterization, supply the quantities as summary input.

Relative to the Saturated Model

Bollen et al. (2014) report each criterion as the difference between the hypothesized model and the saturated model, so that BIC becomes \(T - df\log N\) for the likelihood ratio statistic \(T\) on \(df\) degrees of freedom. Subtracting the saturated model's criterion from the hypothesized model's gives that scale. A single model's criterion cannot be reconstructed from \(T\) and \(df\) alone.

References

Akaike, H. (1974). A new look at the statistical model identification. IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 19(6), 716–723. doi:10.1109/TAC.1974.1100705

Asparouhov, T. (2005). Sampling weights in latent variable modeling. Structural Equation Modeling, 12(3), 411–434.

Bollen, K. A., Harden, J. J., Ray, S., & Zavisca, J. (2014). BIC and alternative Bayesian information criteria in the selection of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling, 21(1), 1–19. doi:10.1080/10705511.2014.856691

Bollen, K. A., Ray, S., Zavisca, J., & Harden, J. J. (2012). A comparison of Bayes factor approximation methods including two new methods. Sociological Methods & Research, 41(2), 294–324. doi:10.1177/0049124112452393

Burnham, K. P., & Anderson, D. R. (2004). Multimodel inference: Understanding AIC and BIC in model selection. Sociological Methods & Research, 33(2), 261–304. doi:10.1177/0049124104268644

Haughton, D. M. A. (1988). On the choice of a model to fit data from an exponential family. The Annals of Statistics, 16(1), 342–355. doi:10.1214/aos/1176350709

Lai, K. (2021). Using information criteria under missing data: Full information maximum likelihood versus two-stage estimation. Structural Equation Modeling, 28(2), 278–291. doi:10.1080/10705511.2020.1780925

Lin, L.-C., Huang, P.-H., & Weng, L.-J. (2017). Selecting path models in SEM: A comparison of model selection criteria. Structural Equation Modeling, 24(6), 855–869. doi:10.1080/10705511.2017.1363652

Rissanen, J. (1978). Modeling by shortest data description. Automatica, 14(5), 465–471. doi:10.1016/0005-1098(78)90005-5

Schwarz, G. (1978). Estimating the dimension of a model. The Annals of Statistics, 6(2), 461–464. doi:10.1214/aos/1176344136

Sclove, S. L. (1987). Application of model-selection criteria to some problems in multivariate analysis. Psychometrika, 52(3), 333–343. doi:10.1007/BF02294360

compare_sem to compare fitted models by one of these criteria, sem_fit_measures for the fit measures of one model, and the vignette vignette("sem_fit_measures", package = "DMAR").

Examples

# The three-factor model of nine of the holzinger_swineford
# tests, identified by a marker indicator (lavaan's default).
fit <- lavaan::cfa(
  "visual  =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
   textual =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning
   speed   =~ t10_addition + t12_counting_groups_of_dots +
              t13_straight_and_curved_capitals",
  data = holzinger_swineford)
sem_information_criteria(fit)
#>  term           value    
#>  AIC            19198.131
#>  BIC            19275.980
#>  SABIC          19209.380
#>  HBIC           19237.384
#>  IBIC           <NA>     
#>  SPBIC          <NA>     
#>  log_likelihood -9578.065
#>  npar           21       
#>  N              301      
#> 
#> Smaller is preferred; only a difference between models fitted to the same data under the same likelihood is meaningful.
#> Not requested: IBIC, SPBIC (see 'measures').
#> Log likelihood: the normal log likelihood of the complete data.
sem_information_criteria(fit, measures = c("BIC", "IBIC", "SPBIC"))
#>  term           value    
#>  AIC            <NA>     
#>  BIC            19275.980
#>  SABIC          <NA>     
#>  HBIC           <NA>     
#>  IBIC           19101.759
#>  SPBIC          19259.359
#>  log_likelihood -9578.065
#>  npar           21       
#>  N              301      
#> 
#> Smaller is preferred; only a difference between models fitted to the same data under the same likelihood is meaningful.
#> Not requested: AIC, SABIC, HBIC (see 'measures').
#> Log likelihood: the normal log likelihood of the complete data.
#> IBIC and SPBIC depend on how the latent variables are identified (here marker indicator) and on the mean structure, IBIC also on the units; compare only models that share them.
#> SPBIC prior: Bollen et al. (2014, p. 6): free loadings and regression coefficients centered at zero, other free parameters at their estimates; Q = 1053.78, dimension 21.

# Summary input: the autoregressive model of Bollen et al. (2014,
# Table 6), whose BIC relative to the saturated model is T - df log N.
ar <- sem_information_criteria(log_likelihood = -534.27 / 2, npar = 14,
                               N = 3912)
saturated <- sem_information_criteria(log_likelihood = 0, npar = 20,
                                      N = 3912)
ar$value[ar$term == "BIC"] - saturated$value[saturated$term == "BIC"]
#> [1] 484.6392

# SPBIC from summary input, with an explicit prior mean.
sem_information_criteria(log_likelihood = -120, npar = 2, N = 200,
                         measures = "SPBIC",
                         parameter_estimate = c(0.4, 1),
                         prior_mean = c(0, 1),
                         information_observed = diag(c(100, 50)))
#>  term           value   
#>  AIC            <NA>    
#>  BIC            <NA>    
#>  SABIC          <NA>    
#>  HBIC           <NA>    
#>  IBIC           <NA>    
#>  SPBIC          246.159 
#>  log_likelihood -120.000
#>  npar           2       
#>  N              200     
#> 
#> Smaller is preferred; only a difference between models fitted to the same data under the same likelihood is meaningful.
#> Not requested: AIC, BIC, SABIC, HBIC, IBIC (see 'measures').
#> SPBIC depends on how the latent variables are identified and on the mean structure; compare only models that share them.
#> SPBIC prior: explicit prior mean; Q = 16, dimension 2.
